note:
A DE moment is a point at which the direction should change. The practitioner named it on 2026-10-15, after finding that a map still had an Input mode a day after the discussion that ruled against modes: "The map output discussion is what we call a DE moment, a moment when things should head in a different direction, and it did not."

This file is the answer to that. Every direction a discussion settles is recorded here with what it requires IN CODE and a clock on it, because the failure mode is specific and this project has produced it at least three times: the direction is written into a spec page, a glossary entry or an ontology term, the code is left alone, and the record now says the matter is settled while the running application still does the old thing. A widget page is not a work item and no ratchet can see one.

It is deliberately not the blocker ledger. A blocker is a claim that something CANNOT be done yet. A direction is a decision that something SHOULD now be done differently, and the two fail in opposite ways: a blocker rots by being lifted and not noticed, a direction rots by being agreed and not built.
windowBasis: The same window the blocker ledger uses, for the same reason: this project changes in days. A direction nobody has checked in a week is a direction nobody is acting on, and saying so is the entire point of the file.

A design constraint, and it rules things OUT. Fieldwork enforces what happens inside a run and nothing beyond it: whether a step produces output, what a receipt says, whose words a reader is shown. It does not enforce what a practitioner does with a figure, whether an obligation is honoured at a venue, or whether prose written by a ruleset author is any good. Mechanisms that pretend otherwise are to be refused, because a false boundary is worse than an acknowledged gap -- it reads as a guarantee and is not one.

The instance that produced this, same day: the obligation text on a ruleset was designed NOT EDITABLE, so a practitioner could not soften an obligation a dataset's authors impose. The practitioner struck it down: "they could soften it as much as they can, but the hard constraint and the accountability to audience and the consequences of shirking that responsibility will always make them think twice -- the consequences are real, even if they manage to skirt around the responsibility: non-acceptance of a publication, questioning by peers during a presentation." Locking the text stopped nobody determined and confused editorial control with enforcement. What replaced it is attribution: the author's wording stays pinned, an edit is recorded as the practitioner's revision in the receipt, and a reader can see whose words they are reading. That is the whole of what an application can honestly protect.

Three layers, and only two are Fieldwork's: STRUCTURAL -- no connection, no output, unaffected by any rewrite; ATTRIBUTIONAL -- whose words a reader is seeing; and CONSEQUENTIAL -- a paper not accepted, a question nobody can answer, which is not Fieldwork's to grant and is the one that governs.

Every epidemiological measure is then a function of that table: rate ratio, risk ratio, odds ratio, rate difference, attributable fraction, and a stratified estimate across a third variable. Each declares its estimator and its interval method ON THE RESULT, because "the 95% interval" is not one thing.

THE EVIDENCE IS THIS SESSION'S OWN WORK. rate_ratio was admitted and built on 2026-10-25 as a widget that computes ONE statistic -- a statistic wearing a node type, which is the same shape as `alert` being a declaration wearing one, retired the same week for exactly that. Adding risk ratio, odds ratio, rate difference and a Mantel-Haenszel stratified estimate as widgets would be five more palette entries against a target of 41, each carrying its own copy of the counts, the direction parameter, the interval machinery and the assumptions. The second one would already be a duplicate under D2.

The framing exists here already: experiment 65 settled that apply_ruleset is an INTERPRETER and a ruleset is a PROGRAM, so one widget serves many declared behaviours. A kernel is that shape for measurement rather than for rules -- one widget, a declared measure, the method named on the result.

What it must carry, from the distinctions already paid for: a rate is not a risk (Poisson admits more events than units, binomial does not, and rate.ts's `rateKind` already decides which); a ratio is dimensionless and the multiplier cancels; a zero cell has no interval and adding half an event is an assumption; an interval is not a p-value; and a Poisson interval treats events as independent, which a transmitted disease is not.

THE PARADIGM DIFFERENCE DECIDES WHERE THE NARRATIVE LIVES. A procedural analysis is a program read top to bottom: the command sequence IS the account of what was done, and its output stream follows the same order, so a reader who has the program has the story. A visual analysis is a GRAPH. A graph has no first line. Nothing about a canvas says where to start reading, which branch mattered, or why one group was compared with another rather than the reverse -- and none of that is recoverable from the topology.

So the narrative has to be CARRIED rather than implied, and that is what the notes are for. They are not annotation on the work; in a visual language they do the job the command sequence does in a procedural one. The unit of story is the PROJECT: South London is five workflows that together make Snow's argument -- rates, the ground, 1849 against 1854, the choropleth, the water companies -- and each is a section rather than a separate analysis. A reader opening it should be able to follow it in an order somebody chose.

WHAT THIS NEEDS, none of it built: a project that declares its own order and says what each workflow contributes; a note that travels with a result rather than living beside it in a parameter a figure may or may not show; and a way for a reader to move through a project as a sequence, which today they cannot -- the workflow selector is a list with no stated order and no account of why one comes after another.

WHAT TO LEARN FROM THE PROCEDURAL SIDE, examined 2026-10-26: its results are typed records that declare their own operation, the plan version that produced them, the canonical source they ran on, and what they DID NOT USE -- records excluded for missing values, for invalid weights, for zero weight. A result that says what it dropped is a result a reader can audit. Fieldwork's receipts carry provenance well and its outputs carry much less; the shape worth borrowing is the result that accounts for its own inputs, which `authoredDataIssues` already does for one case and nothing does generally.

They do not need Fieldwork to reproduce a particular implementation's floating point, and the cost of trying is specific rather than theoretical: epi-info-ai's own contract carries six method identifiers containing `legacy`, and its method contract records that `legacyBreslowDayOddsRatio` directly ports `Single2x2.bdOR`, a Woolf weighted log-odds dispersion THAT THE LEGACY OUTPUT LABELS 'Breslow-Day test for Odds'. A table drawn in the taught layout, with a rate ratio beside it where a risk ratio is expected, will be read as the risk ratio. The resolution is to do both rather than choose: compute and NAME the statistic honestly, and state what Epi Info calls it, so a trained reader finds what they were taught to look for and learns where the taught label is loose. checks.found: Stated and recorded the same day, and it ANSWERS the question experiment 147 had left open. 147 weighed a blank table shell against detection of incoming columns; this is neither. The design names the computations, the computations carry their own equation terms, and the import maps columns onto those terms -- so nothing is invented and nothing is guessed. It also dodges 147's recorded objection that a role is not a property of a column: the term belongs to the EQUATION, and the mapping says which column plays it in which computation, so one column can be a denominator in one and a numerator in another. And the term lists already exist written longhand, as the parameters of `two_by_two` (exposureColumn, exposed, unexposed, outcomeColumn, caseValue, nonCaseValue) and `rate` (numeratorField, denominatorField, denominatorUnit). One shape of mine was backwards and is corrected here: a design cannot be a pass-through threaded between a table and its computation, because the mapping happens AT table input, so the design is upstream of everything like `study_area` is. Two mechanisms follow -- the design travels on a port to the computations it gates, and the import dialog finds it by walking the workflow, which is what `declaredKinds(workflow, nodeId)` and `upstreamKeyValues` already do. One gap found while writing this down: a machined title needs a study PERIOD, and nothing declares one at workflow level -- `rate` has numeratorPeriod and denominatorVintage and `case_series` has a period, all of which are properties of a computation rather than of the study, which is backwards for a title.
